english: The coffee? I drink it without sugar.
explanation_or_example: El café is masculine singular, and a direct object pronoun copies its gender and number, so lo. La would replace a feminine noun, like la leche.

english: The soup? My son never eats it.
explanation_or_example: La sopa is feminine singular, so the direct object pronoun is la. Lo is for masculine nouns, like el pan.

english: The new shoes? Ana is wearing them today.
explanation_or_example: Los zapatos is masculine plural, so the pronoun is los. Las would replace a feminine plural noun, like las botas.

spanish: ¿Las llaves? Pablo ___ tiene en el bolsillo.
english: The keys? Pablo has them in his pocket.
explanation_or_example: Las llaves is feminine plural, so las, even though Pablo is a man. The pronoun takes the gender of the thing, not of the person who has it.

spanish: Compré una revista y ___ leí en el tren.
english: I bought a magazine and read it on the train.
explanation_or_example: Una revista is what I read, the direct object, and it is feminine singular, so la. Lo would need a masculine noun, like un periódico.

spanish: Tengo dos entradas, pero no ___ necesito.
english: I have two tickets, but I don't need them.
explanation_or_example: Dos entradas is feminine plural (las entradas), so las. The order is no, then the pronoun, then the verb: no las necesito.

english: Where is the remote? I can't find it.
explanation_or_example: El mando, from the previous sentence, is masculine singular, so lo. La would need a feminine noun, like la llave.

spanish: Esta película es muy buena; yo ___ vi el sábado.
english: This film is very good; I saw it on Saturday.
explanation_or_example: Esta película is feminine singular, so la. Lo would mean you saw something masculine, such as el partido.

spanish: Hay galletas en la mesa, pero los niños no ___ quieren.
english: There are biscuits on the table, but the children don't want them.
explanation_or_example: Galletas is feminine plural, so las. Los niños just before the blank is who wants them, and the pronoun agrees with what is wanted.

english: The homework? I already finished it.
explanation_or_example: Los deberes is the thing I finished, a direct object, so los. Les is an indirect pronoun for people who receive something.

spanish: El pan está duro; ¿por qué no ___ tiras?
english: The bread is hard; why don't you throw it away?
explanation_or_example: El pan is masculine singular, so lo. La would need a feminine noun, like la fruta.

spanish: La maleta ya está lista; mi padre ___ lleva al coche.
english: The suitcase is ready; my father is taking it to the car.
explanation_or_example: La maleta is feminine singular, so la. Mi padre is masculine, but the pronoun agrees with the thing carried, not the person carrying it.

spanish: ¿El coche? Carlos ___ aparca siempre en la calle.
english: The car? Carlos always parks it on the street.
explanation_or_example: El coche is masculine singular, so lo. Coche ends in -e, so the article el, not the ending, tells you the gender.

spanish: ¿Tienes las gafas? No, ___ dejé en casa.
english: Do you have the glasses? No, I left them at home.
explanation_or_example: Las gafas is always plural in Spanish, even for one pair, so las. Los would only work for a masculine plural noun, like los guantes.

spanish: ¿Quieres probar estas manzanas? Yo ya ___ probé.
english: Do you want to try these apples? I already tried them.
explanation_or_example: Estas manzanas is feminine plural, as estas shows, so las. Los would need a masculine noun, like estos plátanos.

spanish: Hice una tarta y mis amigos ___ probaron enseguida.
english: I made a cake and my friends tried it straight away.
explanation_or_example: Una tarta is feminine singular, so la. Mis amigos is the subject doing the tasting, so it does not affect the pronoun.

spanish: ¿Las noticias? Siempre ___ escuchamos en la radio.
english: The news? We always listen to it on the radio.
explanation_or_example: Las noticias is feminine plural and is the thing we listen to, so las. Les is an indirect pronoun for people, never for things.

spanish: Mi abuela me llama y yo ___ visito los domingos.
english: My grandmother calls me and I visit her on Sundays.
explanation_or_example: Visitar takes a direct object, and mi abuela is feminine singular, so la. Lo would be for a man, like mi abuelo.

spanish: Juan está en la estación. ¿Tú ___ recoges?
english: Juan is at the station. Will you pick him up?
explanation_or_example: Recoger a alguien takes a direct object, and Juan is a man, so lo. La would be for a woman.

english: "Can you hear me well?" "Yes, I can hear you perfectly."
explanation_or_example: ¿Me oyes bien? asks about me, so in the reply the person heard is you: te. Me would mean I can hear myself.

spanish: Cuando llegamos tarde, el profesor ___ mira con cara seria.
english: When we arrive late, the teacher looks at us with a serious face.
explanation_or_example: Llegamos shows the speaker means nosotros, so the people the teacher looks at are us: nos. Los would mean them.

english: My parents love me a lot.
explanation_or_example: Mis padres love me, and me is the object pronoun for yo. Mí is only used after a preposition, as in a mí.

spanish: Mis primos viven lejos y casi nunca ___ veo.
english: My cousins live far away and I almost never see them.
explanation_or_example: Mis primos is masculine plural, so los, and a mixed group of cousins also takes los. Las would only fit a group of women, like mis primas.

spanish: Ana y Lucía ___ invitaron a su boda.
english: Ana and Lucía invited us to their wedding.
explanation_or_example: Ana y Lucía are the ones inviting, and the people invited are us, so nos. Los would mean them.

spanish: Mi hermana es muy simpática; todos ___ adoran.
english: My sister is very friendly; everyone adores her.
explanation_or_example: Adorar takes a direct object, and mi hermana is feminine singular, so la. Le is for indirect objects, the person who receives something.

english: If you have problems, I'll help you.
explanation_or_example: Si tienes problemas shows the person helped is you, so te. Ti only appears after a preposition.

spanish: Cuando éramos pequeños, nuestros abuelos ___ llevaban al parque.
english: When we were little, our grandparents took us to the park.
explanation_or_example: Éramos (we were) shows the people taken to the park are us, so nos. Los would mean other people.

english: "Will you wait for me?" "Yes, I'll wait for you at the door."
explanation_or_example: ¿Me esperas? asks about waiting for me, so in the reply the speaker waits for you: te. Me would mean waiting for yourself.

english: Our friends call us every week.
explanation_or_example: Nuestros amigos are the ones calling, and the people called are us, so nos. Los would make them the people called.

english: The photos? I still haven't seen them.
explanation_or_example: Las fotos is feminine plural, so las, and in a compound tense it goes before haber: no las he visto.

spanish: ¿El correo de Sonia? Ya ___ he leído.
english: Sonia's email? I've already read it.
explanation_or_example: El correo is a masculine singular direct object, so lo goes before haber: lo he leído.

english: And the letter? Nobody has opened it.
explanation_or_example: La carta is feminine singular, so la goes before haber: la ha abierto.

spanish: ¿Los platos? Mi hermano ya ___ ha lavado.
english: The dishes? My brother has already washed them.
explanation_or_example: Los platos is masculine plural, so los goes before haber: los ha lavado.

spanish: Ese chico ___ está mirando desde la ventana.
english: That guy is looking at you from the window.
explanation_or_example: Ese chico is looking at you, so te. With estar + gerund the pronoun can go before estar: te está mirando.

spanish: ¿El partido? Nosotros ___ estamos viendo en casa de Luis.
english: The match? We're watching it at Luis's place.
explanation_or_example: El partido is a masculine singular direct object, so lo, which can go before estar: lo estamos viendo.

spanish: ¿Las flores? Mi madre ___ va a poner en la mesa.
english: The flowers? My mother is going to put them on the table.
explanation_or_example: Las flores is feminine plural, so las. With ir a + infinitive it can go before the conjugated verb: las va a poner.

english: The book? I'm reading it right now.
explanation_or_example: El libro gives lo, attached to the gerund: leyendo + lo = leyéndolo. The written accent keeps the stress on the same syllable.

spanish: ¿La cena? Mi padre está ___ en la cocina.
english: Dinner? My father is making it in the kitchen.
explanation_or_example: La cena is feminine, so la: preparándola. Preparándolo would mean preparing something masculine, like el desayuno.

english: The exercises? We're still doing them with the teacher.
explanation_or_example: Los ejercicios is masculine plural, so haciéndolos. Haciéndolas would need a feminine noun, like las tareas.

english: The shirts? I'm ironing them now.
explanation_or_example: Las camisas gives las: planchando + las = planchándolas. Attaching a pronoun to a gerund always needs a written accent.

english: Your brother? I'm calling him right now.
explanation_or_example: Tu hermano gives lo: llamando + lo = llamándolo. The accent keeps the stress on -man-.

english: This jacket? I want to buy it today.
explanation_or_example: Esta chaqueta is feminine, so la attaches to the infinitive: comprarla. One pronoun on an infinitive needs no accent.

spanish: ¿Los documentos? Tienes que ___ antes del viernes.
english: The documents? You have to sign them before Friday.
explanation_or_example: Los documentos is masculine plural, so firmarlos. Firmarlas would need a feminine noun, like las cartas.

spanish: Mi amiga llega a las seis y voy a ___ al aeropuerto.
english: My friend arrives at six and I'm going to pick her up at the airport.
explanation_or_example: Buscar a alguien takes a direct object, and mi amiga is a woman, so buscarla. Le is for indirect objects.

spanish: ¿El piso? Van a ___ el mes que viene.
english: The flat? They're going to sell it next month.
explanation_or_example: El piso is masculine singular, so venderlo. Venderla would need a feminine noun, like la casa.

spanish: "¿Sabes que Carla se muda?" "Sí, ya ___ sé."
english: "Do you know that Carla is moving?" "Yes, I already know."
explanation_or_example: Lo stands for the whole idea that Carla se muda. A whole idea is always lo.

spanish: "¿Es verdad que cierran el museo?" "No ___ creo."
english: "Is it true that they're closing the museum?" "I don't think so."
explanation_or_example: Neuter lo replaces the whole statement that cierran el museo: no lo creo.

spanish: A su hermana ___ vi ayer en el mercado.
english: I saw his sister yesterday at the market.
explanation_or_example: A su hermana is a direct object placed before the verb, so Spanish repeats it with la: a su hermana la vi.

spanish: Los tomates ___ compré en el mercado.
english: I bought the tomatoes at the market.
explanation_or_example: Los tomates is a direct object placed before the verb, so los repeats it: los tomates los compré.

spanish: Esa canción ___ canta todo el mundo.
english: Everyone sings that song.
explanation_or_example: Esa canción is the direct object placed first, so la repeats it. Todo el mundo is the subject doing the singing.

spanish: Mañana es el cumpleaños de mi madre y ___ voy a regalar flores.
english: Tomorrow is my mother's birthday and I'm going to give her flowers.
explanation_or_example: Mi madre receives the flowers, so she is the indirect object: le. La would make your mother the thing being given.

spanish: ¿Qué ___ vas a decir a tu jefe?
english: What are you going to tell your boss?
explanation_or_example: A tu jefe receives the message, so the indirect pronoun is le. A tu jefe clarifies who le refers to.

spanish: Mis alumnos ___ escriben correos a menudo.
english: My students often write emails to me.
explanation_or_example: Mis alumnos write emails to me, so I am the indirect object: me. Mi without an accent means my.

spanish: ¿Quién ___ explicó la lección a los niños?
english: Who explained the lesson to the children?
explanation_or_example: A los niños receives the explanation, so the plural indirect pronoun is les, even with a los niños also in the sentence.

spanish: Ana ___ prestó su bicicleta a Carlos.
english: Ana lent her bike to Carlos.
explanation_or_example: A Carlos is who gets the bike, the indirect object, so le. Lo would make Carlos the thing being lent.

spanish: Cuando viajo, ___ mando postales a mis padres.
english: When I travel, I send postcards to my parents.
explanation_or_example: A mis padres is who receives the postcards, so the indirect pronoun is les. Los would mean you post your parents themselves.

english: Did your brother give the money back to you?
explanation_or_example: El dinero comes back to you, so you are the indirect object: te. Ti only appears after a preposition, as in a ti.

english: The waiter brought us the bill.
explanation_or_example: La cuenta is what is brought, and we get it, so the indirect pronoun is nos. Los is a direct pronoun and means them.

spanish: Siempre ___ cuento mis secretos a mi mejor amiga.
english: I always tell my secrets to my best friend.
explanation_or_example: A mi mejor amiga is the person told, the indirect object, so le, for women as well as men.

spanish: La profesora ___ preguntó a los estudiantes por el examen.
english: The teacher asked the students about the exam.
explanation_or_example: Preguntar a alguien takes an indirect object, and a los estudiantes is plural, so les.

spanish: Tengo frío; ¿tú ___ puedes dar una manta?
english: I'm cold; can you give me a blanket?
explanation_or_example: Una manta is the thing given, and I am the one who gets it, so the indirect pronoun is me. Mi without an accent means my.

spanish: El médico ___ recetó unas pastillas a mi padre.
english: The doctor prescribed some pills for my father.
explanation_or_example: Unas pastillas is what is prescribed, and a mi padre is who gets it, so the indirect pronoun le. Lo would make your father the thing prescribed.

spanish: ¿Qué ___ pasa a Lucía? Está muy callada.
english: What's wrong with Lucía? She's very quiet.
explanation_or_example: Pasar works like gustar here, so a Lucía is the indirect object: le, even for a woman. La would be a direct object pronoun.

spanish: Los vecinos ___ pidieron silencio a los estudiantes del piso de arriba.
english: The neighbours asked the students upstairs to be quiet.
explanation_or_example: Pedir treats the person asked as an indirect object, and a los estudiantes is plural, so les, not los.

spanish: Yo ___ escribo todos los días, pero tú nunca contestas.
english: I write to you every day, but you never answer.
explanation_or_example: The person written to is you, as tú nunca contestas shows, and escribir a alguien takes an indirect object: te. Ti only follows a preposition.

spanish: Nuestros padres ___ dieron una sorpresa el fin de semana.
english: Our parents gave us a surprise at the weekend.
explanation_or_example: Una sorpresa is what is given, and we receive it, so the indirect pronoun is nos. Los would mean them, and it is a direct pronoun.

spanish: Cuando llegó el cartero, ___ di una propina.
english: When the postman arrived, I gave him a tip.
explanation_or_example: Una propina is what is given, and el cartero is who gets it, so le. Lo would make the postman the thing given.

spanish: ¿Por qué no ___ compras un regalo a tu hermana?
english: Why don't you buy your sister a present?
explanation_or_example: A tu hermana is who the present is for, the indirect object. Indirect pronouns do not change for gender, so le, not la.

spanish: A mis hijos ___ encanta el helado.
english: My children love ice cream.
explanation_or_example: Encantar works like gustar, so a mis hijos is the indirect object, and plural: les.

spanish: A nosotros ___ interesa mucho la historia.
english: We're very interested in history.
explanation_or_example: Interesar works like gustar, and a nosotros points to us, so nos.

spanish: ¿Ya ___ mandaste las fotos a tus primos?
english: Did you already send the photos to your cousins?
explanation_or_example: Las fotos is what is sent, and a tus primos receive them, so the plural indirect pronoun is les. Los would replace a plural thing.

spanish: El jefe ___ ofreció un contrato nuevo a Elena.
english: The boss offered Elena a new contract.
explanation_or_example: A Elena is who gets the offer, the indirect object, so le even for a woman. La would treat Elena as the thing offered.

spanish: La tienda ___ devolvió el dinero a los clientes.
english: The shop gave the customers their money back.
explanation_or_example: El dinero is returned to a los clientes, the indirect object, so les. Los would replace a plural thing being returned.

english: My boyfriend always brings me flowers.
explanation_or_example: Mi novio brings flowers to me, so I am the indirect object: me. Mi without an accent means my, as in mi novio.

spanish: Ella nunca ___ dice mentiras a sus amigos.
english: She never tells her friends lies.
explanation_or_example: Mentiras is what is told, and a sus amigos is who hears it, so les. Los would replace a masculine plural thing.

spanish: El guía ___ está explicando la historia del castillo a los turistas.
english: The guide is explaining the history of the castle to the tourists.
explanation_or_example: A los turistas receive the explanation, so les. With estar + gerund it can go before estar.

spanish: ¿Qué ___ regalaste a tu novia por su cumpleaños?
english: What did you give your girlfriend for her birthday?
explanation_or_example: A tu novia is who gets the present, the indirect object, so le. Le is used for men and women alike.

spanish: Cuando era niño, mi madre ___ leía cuentos cada noche.
english: When I was a child, my mother read me stories every night.
explanation_or_example: Cuando era niño shows the stories were read to me, so the indirect pronoun is me. Mi without an accent means my.

spanish: ¿Ya ___ contaste a tus padres lo del viaje?
english: Have you told your parents about the trip yet?
explanation_or_example: A tus padres are the people told, an indirect object, so les, not the direct los.

spanish: Los abuelos ___ dejaron la casa a sus nietos.
english: The grandparents left the house to their grandchildren.
explanation_or_example: La casa is what is left, and a sus nietos receive it, so les, not los.

english: Do you want me to lend you my car?
explanation_or_example: Mi coche is lent to you, so the indirect pronoun is te. Ti never stands alone before a verb.

spanish: El profesor ___ puso una mala nota a Pedro.
english: The teacher gave Pedro a bad mark.
explanation_or_example: Una mala nota is the direct object, and a Pedro is the indirect object, so le. Lo would make Pedro the thing given.

spanish: Los niños ___ piden dulces a su abuela.
english: The children ask their grandmother for sweets.
explanation_or_example: Pedir treats the person asked as an indirect object, so a su abuela takes le even for a woman. La would be wrong.

spanish: Mi jefe no ___ ha contestado todavía.
english: My boss hasn't answered me yet.
explanation_or_example: Mi jefe has not answered me, and contestar a alguien takes an indirect object, so me before haber. Mi without an accent means my.

spanish: Señora García, ___ traigo los documentos que pidió.
english: Mrs García, I'm bringing you the documents you asked for.
explanation_or_example: Señora García is usted, the person receiving the documents, and usted as an indirect object is le, for women as well as men.

spanish: El dentista ___ sacó una muela a mi hermano.
english: The dentist pulled one of my brother's teeth.
explanation_or_example: A mi hermano is the person affected, and Spanish marks that with the indirect pronoun le.

spanish: Hoy ___ toca a ti fregar los platos.
english: Today it's your turn to wash the dishes.
explanation_or_example: Tocar (to be someone's turn) takes an indirect object: te toca. A ti adds emphasis but never replaces te.

spanish: A ella ___ dieron el premio, no a él.
english: They gave the prize to her, not to him.
explanation_or_example: A ella clarifies and contrasts, but the indirect pronoun le must still appear.

english: I owe you an explanation.
explanation_or_example: A usted is the person owed, so the indirect pronoun is le. The a + person phrase only adds clarity.

spanish: A ustedes ___ mando la información por correo.
english: I'll send you all the information by email.
explanation_or_example: A ustedes receives the information, an indirect object, so les. Ustedes as an indirect object is always les, never los.

spanish: Voy a ___ un mensaje a Marta.
english: I'm going to write Marta a message.
explanation_or_example: A Marta receives the message, so le attaches to the infinitive: escribirle. La would be wrong for a receiver.

spanish: Estoy ___ la verdad a mis padres.
english: I'm telling my parents the truth.
explanation_or_example: La verdad is what is said, and a mis padres hear it, so les attaches to the gerund: diciéndoles.

english: Can you pass me the salt, please?
explanation_or_example: La sal is passed to the speaker, so the pronoun is me: pasarme. Pasarte would mean passing it to yourself.

english: I need to ask you a question, teacher.
explanation_or_example: Profesora is the usted being asked, so le attaches: hacerle. Una pregunta is the direct object.

spanish: Estamos ___ una carta a los Reyes Magos.
english: We're writing a letter to the Three Kings.
explanation_or_example: A los Reyes Magos is who the letter is written to, an indirect object, so les attaches: escribiéndoles.

english: The book? My brother lent it to me yesterday.
explanation_or_example: With two pronouns the person comes first, then the thing: me (to me) + lo (el libro) = me lo. Lo me is never possible.

english: The photo? I'll send it to you now.
explanation_or_example: Indirect comes before direct: te (to you) + la (la foto) = te la. La te is the wrong order.

english: The dessert? The waiter will bring it to us right away.
explanation_or_example: Indirect comes before direct: nos (to us) + lo (el postre) = nos lo. Lo nos is the wrong order.

spanish: ¿Las fotos del viaje? Ana ___ enseñó ayer.
english: The trip photos? Ana showed them to us yesterday.
explanation_or_example: Las fotos is feminine even though foto ends in -o (short for la fotografía), so nos las, not nos los.

english: My pen? Yes, I'll give it back to you now.
explanation_or_example: Mi bolígrafo is masculine (el bolígrafo), so the thing is lo: te lo. Te la would need a feminine noun, like la goma.

spanish: ¿Quién te regaló esa bufanda? Mi abuela ___ regaló.
english: Who gave you that scarf? My grandmother gave it to me.
explanation_or_example: Me comes first because I received it, and esa bufanda is feminine, so me la. Me lo would need something masculine, like el gorro.

spanish: Si necesitas el coche, yo ___ presto.
english: If you need the car, I'll lend it to you.
explanation_or_example: Si necesitas shows the person is tú, so the pair is te lo. Se only replaces le or les.

spanish: El profesor explicó el ejercicio a Marta y luego ___ explicó a mí.
english: The teacher explained the exercise to Marta and then explained it to me.
explanation_or_example: A mí points to me, so the pair is me lo. Se only replaces le or les.

spanish: ¿La receta? Mi tía ___ dio a nosotras.
english: The recipe? My aunt gave it to us.
explanation_or_example: A nosotras means us, so the indirect pronoun is nos, not se. Only le and les turn into se.

spanish: ¿Los billetes? Yo ___ compro a ti si quieres.
english: The tickets? I'll buy them for you if you want.
explanation_or_example: A ti points to tú, so the pair is te los. Se only replaces le or les.

english: The glasses? Mum has put them away for you.
explanation_or_example: Las gafas is feminine plural, so te las, placed before haber as a block. Te los would need a masculine noun, like los guantes.

spanish: ¿La mesa? Mis amigos ___ han vendido a buen precio.
english: The table? My friends have sold it to me at a good price.
explanation_or_example: La mesa is feminine, so me la, placed before haber. Me lo would need a masculine noun, like el sofá.

spanish: ¿El vestido? Mi madre ___ hizo a mí para la boda.
english: The dress? My mother made it for me for the wedding.
explanation_or_example: El vestido is masculine, so me lo, not me la. A mí only adds emphasis; me must still appear.

english: Do you need my dictionary? I'll lend it to you now.
explanation_or_example: Mi diccionario is masculine (el diccionario), so te lo. Te comes first because you receive it.

spanish: ¿Tus padres te compraron la moto? Sí, ___ compraron el año pasado.
english: Did your parents buy you the motorbike? Yes, they bought it for me last year.
explanation_or_example: La moto ends in -o but is feminine (short for la motocicleta), so me la, not me lo.

spanish: ¿Me explicas el problema? Claro, ahora ___ explico.
english: Will you explain the problem to me? Sure, I'll explain it to you now.
explanation_or_example: In ¿Me explicas el problema? me is the person asking, so in the answer it becomes te: te lo. Me lo would mean explaining it to yourself.

spanish: ¿Me das tu dirección? Sí, ___ doy ahora.
english: Will you give me your address? Yes, I'll give it to you now.
explanation_or_example: Tu dirección ends in -ción, and those nouns are feminine, so the pair is te la, not te lo.

spanish: ¿Me prestas tus apuntes? Sí, ___ presto mañana.
english: Will you lend me your notes? Yes, I'll lend them to you tomorrow.
explanation_or_example: Tus apuntes is masculine plural (los apuntes), so te los. Te las would need a feminine noun, like las notas.

spanish: ¿Las llaves? Juan ___ dio a su hermana.
english: The keys? Juan gave them to his sister.
explanation_or_example: Le (a su hermana) + las (the keys) cannot be le las, so le becomes se: se las. A su hermana shows who se refers to.

spanish: ¿El regalo? Nosotros ___ dimos a Pablo ayer.
english: The present? We gave it to Pablo yesterday.
explanation_or_example: Le (a Pablo) + lo (the present) is never le lo: le becomes se, so se lo.

spanish: ¿Los apuntes? Carmen ___ presta a sus compañeros.
english: The notes? Carmen lends them to her classmates.
explanation_or_example: Les (a sus compañeros) + los (los apuntes) becomes se los, because les turns into se before lo, la, los or las.

spanish: ¿La verdad? No ___ dije a mis padres.
english: The truth? I didn't tell it to my parents.
explanation_or_example: Les (a mis padres) + la (la verdad) becomes se la. Spanish never puts le or les right before lo, la, los or las.

spanish: ¿La pregunta? Ya ___ hice a la profesora.
english: The question? I already asked the teacher.
explanation_or_example: Le + la becomes se la, and a la profesora tells you who se means.

english: The money? I'll give it back to you all tomorrow.
explanation_or_example: Les + lo becomes se lo, and a ustedes clarifies that se means you all.

spanish: ¿Las flores? Mi padre ___ compró a mi madre.
english: The flowers? My father bought them for my mother.
explanation_or_example: Le (for a mi madre) + las (las flores) becomes se las. A mi madre at the end shows who se is.

spanish: El médico revisó los resultados y ___ explicó a la paciente despacio.
english: The doctor reviewed the results and explained them slowly to the patient.
explanation_or_example: Le (a la paciente) + los (los resultados) cannot be le los, so le becomes se: se los. A la paciente shows who se refers to.

spanish: ¿El paquete? El cartero ___ entregó a mis vecinos.
english: The parcel? The postman delivered it to my neighbours.
explanation_or_example: Les + lo (el paquete) becomes se lo. Se does not show singular or plural; a mis vecinos does.

spanish: ¿La contraseña? No ___ puedo decir a nadie.
english: The password? I can't tell it to anyone.
explanation_or_example: Le (a nadie) + la becomes se la, and the pair goes before the conjugated verb: no se la puedo decir.

spanish: ¿El informe? Ya ___ he enviado al director.
english: The report? I've already sent it to the director.
explanation_or_example: Le (al director) + lo becomes se lo, placed before haber: se lo he enviado.

spanish: ¿Las noticias? Todavía no ___ han contado a los niños.
english: The news? They haven't told the children yet.
explanation_or_example: Les (a los niños) + las becomes se las, placed before haber: no se las han contado.

spanish: ¿Tu número? Ya ___ he dado a Laura.
english: Your number? I've already given it to Laura.
explanation_or_example: Le (a Laura) becomes se, and tu número is masculine, so the pair is se lo.

spanish: ¿La carta? Mi hermano ___ está escribiendo a su novia.
english: The letter? My brother is writing it to his girlfriend.
explanation_or_example: Le (a su novia) + la becomes se la. With estar + gerund both pronouns can go before estar.

spanish: ¿El secreto? Mis amigos ___ están contando a todo el mundo.
english: The secret? My friends are telling it to everyone.
explanation_or_example: Le (a todo el mundo) + lo (the secret) becomes se lo, placed before estar.

spanish: ¿La tarta? Nosotros ___ vamos a llevar a la abuela.
english: The cake? We're going to take it to grandma.
explanation_or_example: Le (a la abuela) + la becomes se la. With ir a + infinitive the pair can go before the conjugated verb.

spanish: ¿Los juguetes? Mis padres ___ van a comprar a mi hermano.
english: The toys? My parents are going to buy them for my brother.
explanation_or_example: Le (for a mi hermano) + los (the toys) becomes se los, placed before ir.

spanish: ¿El mensaje? Ya ___ mandé a él, no a ella.
english: The message? I already sent it to him, not to her.
explanation_or_example: Le + lo always becomes se lo. Se could mean him, her, you or them, so a él clarifies it.

english: The tickets? I already gave them to you all, didn't I?
explanation_or_example: Les + las becomes se las. A ustedes clarifies who se refers to.

spanish: ¿Le diste las llaves a Mario? Sí, ya ___ di.
english: Did you give the keys to Mario? Yes, I already gave them to him.
explanation_or_example: The question uses le for a Mario. In the answer le meets las (the keys) and becomes se: se las.

spanish: ¿Les mandaste la invitación a tus tíos? No, todavía no ___ he mandado.
english: Did you send the invitation to your aunt and uncle? No, I haven't sent it yet.
explanation_or_example: Les (a tus tíos) + la (la invitación) becomes se la, placed before haber: no se la he mandado.

spanish: ¿Le compraste el pastel a Ana? Sí, ___ compré esta mañana.
english: Did you buy the cake for Ana? Yes, I bought it for her this morning.
explanation_or_example: Le (for a Ana) + lo (el pastel) would be le lo, which Spanish never allows, so se lo.

spanish: ¿Le regalas los pendientes a tu madre? Sí, ___ regalo para su cumpleaños.
english: Are you giving the earrings to your mother? Yes, I'm giving them to her for her birthday.
explanation_or_example: Le becomes se, and los pendientes is masculine plural, so se los. Se las would need a feminine noun, like las pulseras.

spanish: ¿Quién les explicó el problema a los alumnos? La directora ___ explicó.
english: Who explained the problem to the students? The head teacher explained it to them.
explanation_or_example: The question uses les for a los alumnos. In the answer les meets lo (el problema) and becomes se: se lo.

spanish: ¿Le pediste permiso a tu padre? Sí, ___ pedí ayer.
english: Did you ask your father for permission? Yes, I asked him for it yesterday.
explanation_or_example: Lo stands for permiso, and le (a tu padre) cannot come right before lo, so it changes to se: se lo.

spanish: ¿Le devolviste la chaqueta a Sara? Sí, ya ___ devolví.
english: Did you give the jacket back to Sara? Yes, I already gave it back to her.
explanation_or_example: Se is right, so the question is gender: la chaqueta is feminine, so se la. Se lo would need a masculine noun, like el abrigo.

english: The story? I'm reading it to my daughter.
explanation_or_example: Le (a mi hija) becomes se before lo (el cuento): leyendo + se + lo = leyéndoselo. The accent keeps the stress.

spanish: ¿La lección? El profesor está ___ a los alumnos.
english: The lesson? The teacher is explaining it to the students.
explanation_or_example: Les (a los alumnos) becomes se before la (la lección): explicando + se + la = explicándosela.

english: The photos? I'm sending them to you right now.
explanation_or_example: Las fotos is feminine (short for las fotografías), so mandándotelas. Mandándotelos would need a masculine noun, like los vídeos.

english: The menu? The waiter is bringing it to us now.
explanation_or_example: El menú is masculine, so lo: trayéndonoslo. Trayéndonosla would need a feminine noun, like la carta.

spanish: ¿Los regalos? Papá está ___ a los niños.
english: The presents? Dad is giving them to the children.
explanation_or_example: Les (a los niños) becomes se, and los regalos is masculine plural, so dándoselos. Dándoselas would need a feminine noun.

english: The book? I'm going to give it back to you tomorrow.
explanation_or_example: El libro gives lo and the receiver is you: devolver + te + lo = devolvértelo. With two pronouns attached, the infinitive takes an accent.

english: The bike? I want to lend it to my cousin.
explanation_or_example: Le (a mi primo) becomes se before la (la bicicleta): prestar + se + la = prestársela.

spanish: ¿Los documentos? Tengo que ___ al abogado hoy.
english: The documents? I have to send them to the lawyer today.
explanation_or_example: Le (al abogado) becomes se, and los documentos is masculine plural: mandárselos. Mandárselas would need a feminine noun.

english: The song? Can you sing it to me again?
explanation_or_example: La canción ends in -ción, so it is feminine: me + la = cantármela. Cantármelo would need a masculine noun, like el poema.

english: The plan? We want to explain it to our bosses.
explanation_or_example: Les (a nuestros jefes) becomes se, and lo is singular because it stands for el plan: explicárselo.

spanish: Si quieres las fotos, puedo ___ esta noche.
english: If you want the photos, I can send them to you tonight.
explanation_or_example: Las fotos is feminine even though foto ends in -o, so te + las: enviártelas. With two pronouns attached, the infinitive takes an accent.

spanish: Yo no ___ dónde está la estación.
english: I don't know where the station is.
explanation_or_example: Dónde introduces a piece of information, and knowing information uses saber.

english: Do you know what time it is?
explanation_or_example: Qué hora es asks for a fact, the time, and knowing facts uses saber.

spanish: Mi madre ___ el número de teléfono del médico.
english: My mother knows the doctor's phone number.
explanation_or_example: El número de teléfono is a specific piece of information, so saber.

spanish: Por el aviso ___ que la carretera sigue cerrada.
english: We know from the notice that the road is still closed.
explanation_or_example: Que la carretera sigue cerrada is a fact learned from the notice, so saber. Conocer is for people, places and things you are familiar with.

english: The children don't know the answer.
explanation_or_example: La respuesta is information, and knowing information uses saber.

english: Do you know how much the ticket costs?
explanation_or_example: Cuánto cuesta introduces a piece of information, the price, so saber.

english: I know your address by heart.
explanation_or_example: Knowing a fact de memoria (by heart) uses saber.

english: Ana knows why you arrived late.
explanation_or_example: Por qué introduces a reason, a piece of information, so saber.

spanish: ¿Vosotros ___ si el museo abre los lunes?
english: Do you all know if the museum opens on Mondays?
explanation_or_example: Saber si asks whether someone has a piece of information: si el museo abre los lunes.

spanish: No ___ cómo se llama ese actor.
english: I don't know what that actor's name is.
explanation_or_example: Cómo se llama asks for a name as information, so saber.

english: My parents already know the news.
explanation_or_example: La noticia is information, and knowing news uses saber.

spanish: Todo el mundo ___ que el agua hierve a cien grados.
english: Everyone knows that water boils at one hundred degrees.
explanation_or_example: Saber que introduces a known fact: que el agua hierve a cien grados.

english: Do you know who won the match?
explanation_or_example: Quién ganó introduces a piece of information, so saber.

spanish: Yo no ___ nada de este asunto.
english: I don't know anything about this matter.
explanation_or_example: No saber nada de este asunto means having no information about it, so saber.

spanish: El profesor ___ cuándo es la fiesta.
english: The teacher knows when the party is.
explanation_or_example: Cuándo es la fiesta introduces a piece of information, so saber.

spanish: Ellos no ___ adónde vamos el sábado.
english: They don't know where we are going on Saturday.
explanation_or_example: Adónde vamos introduces a piece of information, so saber.

english: We don't know what happened last night.
explanation_or_example: Qué pasó introduces a piece of information, so saber.

english: She knows the date of the exam.
explanation_or_example: La fecha del examen is a fact, and knowing facts uses saber.

english: Do you know the result of the match?
explanation_or_example: El resultado is information, so saber.

english: I know that you are right.
explanation_or_example: Saber que introduces a fact you know: que tienes razón.

english: Carlos knows a lot about history.
explanation_or_example: Saber mucho de historia means having a lot of knowledge about a subject, so saber.

spanish: Mis amigos no ___ lo que pasó.
english: My friends don't know what happened.
explanation_or_example: Lo que pasó is information about what happened, so saber.

spanish: ¿Alguien ___ a qué hora sale el tren?
english: Does anyone know what time the train leaves?
explanation_or_example: A qué hora sale introduces a piece of information, so saber.

spanish: Yo no ___ si Marta viene a cenar.
english: I don't know if Marta is coming to dinner.
explanation_or_example: Saber si asks whether you have a piece of information: si Marta viene a cenar.

spanish: Usted ___ muy bien lo que quiere.
english: You know very well what you want.
explanation_or_example: Lo que quiere is information about what you want, so saber.

spanish: Los turistas no ___ cuál es el autobús correcto.
english: The tourists don't know which bus is the right one.
explanation_or_example: Cuál es introduces a piece of information, so saber.

spanish: Nadie ___ dónde dejó Pablo las llaves.
english: Nobody knows where Pablo left the keys.
